title: Trump Sets 100% Tariff on Generic Drug Imports Starting August 2028, Threatening India's $10.5 Billion Pharma Pipeline
excerpt: Generic drugmakers get a two-year window to move production to the U.S. or face duties that would double to 200% in 2029, putting affordable medicines at risk.
body:
• President Trump announced generic drugs will face 0% tariffs for two years from August 1, 2026, before rates jump to 100% in August 2028 and 200% in August 2029.
  • India, the largest supplier of generic medicines to the U.S. with $10.5 billion in annual pharmaceutical exports, stands to be the hardest hit — over 40% of India's exports to America would be adversely affected.
  • Generic drugs make up more than 90% of U.S. prescriptions; industry groups warn the tariffs could raise costs and create shortages of affordable medicines ranging from antibiotics to cancer drugs.
  • Analysts and trade groups view the announcement as a negotiating opener similar to deals struck with brand-name drugmakers, with the tariffs unlikely to take effect in their current form.

A Two-Year Countdown for Generics

President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that all generic drugs imported into the United States would remain tariff-free for two years starting August 1, 2026. After that grace period, a 100% duty kicks in for one year, followed by 200% tariffs from August 2029 onward.

"This is done in order to RESHORE Generic Pharmaceutical Production into America, with a penalty to those Companies that decide not to build Plant and Equipment within the stated period of time given to them," Trump wrote.

The announcement follows months of internal debate within the administration. Some White House staff had raised concerns about the tariff levels needed to reshore what is inherently a low-cost business, and the knock-on effects for the generic medicines that make up more than 90% of American prescriptions, according to The Wall Street Journal.

India Takes the Biggest Hit

Among U.S. trading partners, India faces the most significant fallout. Pharmaceuticals rank among India's top three exports to America, totaling $10.5 billion in the 2024-25 fiscal year, according to India's Commerce Ministry. With existing levies on steel, aluminum, and autos, the drug tariffs would push the share of India's U.S. exports facing adverse duties past 40%.

The NSE Nifty Pharma index of 20 Indian drugmakers fell as much as 1.9% following the announcement. Lupin closed 4.3% lower, Aurobindo Pharma dropped 3%, and Dr. Reddy's Laboratories and Glenmark Pharmaceuticals both fell around 2%, according to Morningstar.

"This decision will lead to reduced access to generic medicines in the US because they won't be able to make them as affordable. It'll push them into higher pricing."

— Nathan Gray, Senior Research Fellow, University of Adelaide

In the case of birth control alone, roughly 65% of all pill prescriptions in the U.S. in 2024 were manufactured by just two India-based companies — Glenmark Pharmaceuticals and Lupin, according to a Bloomberg analysis of Symphony Health data.

Industry Calls It a Negotiating Move

The Association for Accessible Medicines, the U.S. generic drug lobby, was "very surprised" by Trump's post, said CEO John Murphy III. But the group sees the tariff threat as a jumping-off point for negotiations, similar to the deals the administration struck with brand-name drugmakers to lower prices and boost U.S. manufacturing in exchange for tariff exemptions.

"It's a tweet, it's a catalyst, and we'll see what happens," Murphy said.

J.P. Morgan analysts echoed that view, writing that the proposal "seems unlikely to be implemented in its current form given it could result in cost increases for U.S. patients." Veda Partners analyst Spencer Perlman was more blunt, calling the tariffs "impractical and undesirable politically and economically."

The Reshoring Math Doesn't Add Up

Generic drugmakers operate on far thinner margins than brand-name producers, making it harder to absorb the costs of relocating manufacturing. Vishal Manchanda, an analyst with Systematix Group, noted that establishing a new manufacturing plant typically takes at least three years — longer than Trump's two-year tariff timeline.

Switzerland's Sandoz, one of the world's largest generic producers, saw shares drop 3.9% after the announcement. CEO Richard Saynor had warned earlier that steep tariffs would likely make drugs more expensive and limit patient access. The company said it was "too early to assess the implications" but that it shared "the goal of improving affordability and access to medicines in the United States."

Patient advocacy group Patients For Affordable Drugs offered a starker assessment. "Imposing massive tariffs on generic medicines risk making lower-cost generic drugs millions of Americans rely on more expensive and harder to access," said CEO Merith Basey.

What to Watch

The tariff clock is now ticking, but the outcome remains uncertain. A February trade pact between the U.S. and India stipulated that India would "receive negotiated outcomes with respect to generic pharmaceuticals and ingredients," suggesting room for a carve-out. Companies may also look to diversify away from the U.S. market rather than absorb the costs of reshoring.

For Indian Americans who rely on affordable generic prescriptions — from cholesterol medications to hypertension treatments — the stakes are personal. Whether the tariffs land as threatened or morph into another negotiating lever, the two-year runway has already injected uncertainty into a supply chain that keeps medicine affordable for hundreds of millions.
nri_angle: India is the largest exporter of generic drugs to the U.S., with $10.5 billion in pharmaceutical exports; tariffs would raise medicine costs for millions of Indian Americans and jeopardize a key Indian export sector.
